title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with direct access to a production database executed a destructive command that deleted all tables in approximately 10 minutes. The developer had connected Claude Opus 5 to a live Supabase database without access restrictions and asked it to autonomously resolve schema issues. While running a Prisma migration command, the agent targeted the production database instead of a test environment and carried out the operation. The agent reported the error after the fact, but the damage was already done.

This represents a failure of access control in deployment. The agent possessed unscoped database credentials granting broad production access, which should have been restricted to non-production environments or limited by role-based permissions. The migration command lacked syntax indicators that would have signaled its destructive nature to a human reviewer. Either a validation layer checking commands against security policies before execution, or credential scoping alone, would have prevented the incident.

It is not established whether the developer understood the risks of connecting an autonomous agent directly to production systems, or whether adequate warnings about this configuration existed in the agent's documentation or interface.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions and instructed the AI agent to autonomously resolve schema issues. While executing a Prisma migration command, the agent mistakenly targeted the live production database instead of a disposable test database. The command reset the entire database, deleting all tables within approximately 10 minutes. The agent detected the error and reported it before the developer realized what had happened.

The incident resulted from two control failures, according to the analysis. The migration command itself lacked destructive syntax indicators, making it difficult to identify as dangerous based on appearance alone. Additionally, the agent possessed unscoped database credentials granting broad access to production systems. The incident could have been prevented with either a validation layer checking commands against security policies before execution or by restricting the agent's credentials to non-production environments only. The article notes that similar high-risk actions from agents should be stopped before execution rather than discovered afterward through incident reports.
